claims.assertion: The rider's own message asks to be let out mid-journey (F3, 17:09: "Please stop the car, I want to get out here."), so the dispute is about a mid-ride exit request, not about the fare or the route.

The driver's reply (F4, 17:10: "Sit down or I lock the doors.") is a single instruction given in response to a rider opening a door in motion; the judge must read the words and decide whether they amount to a threat, and there is no policy clause that converts this sentence into an automatic finding against the driver.

A rider attempting to open the door and exit at traffic lights while the trip is in progress is itself a dangerous act on a live carriageway, so the case involves an allegation touching safety of the ride rather than a fare or route overcharge.

Because a threat/intimidation allegation is raised, the correct procedural course is escalation to a human reviewer with a factual summary rather than an automatic ruling, and the driver does not oppose that route.

No money is in dispute: the trip was a fixed-price RydeX fare (complaint: $32.86 quoted up front), the GPS track shows the actual distance 15.4 km against an optimal 15.5 km, i.e. -0.1 km (F1), so no excess distance and no refundable detour mileage exists.

The whole trip was completed and delivered as booked: 15.4 km actual vs 15.5 km optimal (F1) with a duration of 23.7 min against 21.8 min estimated, i.e. +1.9 min (F2), a normal completion with no unexplained stop and no unrecovered deviation.
There is nothing to claw back on the fare side: no off-route segment, no unbilled detour mileage and no traffic-diversion claim arise on this record (F1, F2), so the fare of $32.86 should stand.

The driver has a clean 90-day record — 893 days on the platform, 1038 trips, 0 disputes and 0 upheld (F8) — which is inconsistent with a pattern of intimidating riders and gives no basis for a flag_account action against him.

The rider likewise has no dispute history (F7: 619 days, 0 disputes, 0 upheld), so the conflict is an isolated one-off incident between two otherwise clean accounts, which supports human review over any automated penalty.

weaknesses: The driver's own written words on record are the weakest point of this case: F4 ("Sit down or I lock the doors.") is capable of being read as an intimidation of the rider, and if the judge so reads it under SAFE-1 the case goes to a person regardless of how clean the rest of the record is.

The driver's account of why he spoke (rider tried to open the door at the lights) exists only in his own post-trip statement, F6; the system record contains no door-sensor, in-cabin or camera fact corroborating it, so the 'she opened the door first' justification rests on an uncorroborated statement and may be treated as a claim rather than proof.

F3 shows the rider asked to be let out at 17:09 and the trip nonetheless continued to drop-off at 17:31 (per the trip record), so the other side can argue the driver refused a stop/exit request and effectively held the rider in the car — the +1.9 min duration in F2 gives them a small figure to point at, and RD-3 is the clause they will invoke against the driver's refusal to stop.

Nothing in the driving record helps the driver on the safety point: F1 and F2 show only an ordinary completed trip, so they rebut any fare or route complaint but do not rebut the rider's account of what was said and how she felt.

claims.assertion: The driver's own in-app message to the rider reads "Sit down or I lock the doors" (F4), sent one minute after the rider asked "Please stop the car, I want to get out here" (F3); on its plain words this is a threat/intimidation directed at the passenger, which is exactly the conduct the safety screening rule is written for.

The driver's statement "I told her to sit down for her own safety and drove on" (F6) is his own written retelling after the trip and does not withdraw the words recorded in the chat record (F4); the chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F5), so the threat is recorded, not merely alleged.

On the recorded facts the rider's complaint is that she asked to get out, was refused and was threatened with being locked in while the car kept moving (F3, F4, F6) — a coercion of a passenger in a moving vehicle — which the policy requires be referred to a human decision-maker rather than auto-adjudicated; I therefore ask for escalate with a fact summary, not an automated refund.

The trip was 23.7 min against an estimate of 21.8 min (F2) while the route was actually 0.1 km shorter than optimal (F1), i.e. the extra time was spent in the car after the rider asked to be let out at 17:09 (F3), which is the period over which the rider says she felt unsafe for the whole ride.

For the fact summary the rider's account is corroborated rather than contradicted by the system records: the chat is complete and timestamped (F5), and the rider has 619 days of account history, a 4.8 rating and no disputes in 90 days (F7), so she is not a serial or opportunistic complainant.

The driver's record is clean on disputes (893 days, 4.62 rating, 1038 trips, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days, F8), so I do not ask for any account flag under this case; the referral to a human is about what happened in the cabin (F4), not about a pattern that the profile data would have to establish.

weaknesses: The threat is recorded in only one line of chat (F4) and the 'lock me in' element of the complaint is the rider's own characterisation of it; a judge could read 'Sit down or I lock the doors' as a safety instruction rather than a threat, though the driver's statement (F6) confirms he refused to stop and drove on.

There is no evidence of dangerous driving, collision or injury in the fact set: gps facts F1 and F2 show a normal route slightly shorter than optimal and only 1.9 min longer than estimated, so the driver can argue the ride was uneventful and no SAFE-2 escalation is triggered.

The rider opened the door at traffic lights on the driver's account (F6) — the other side will use this to frame the message as a legitimate passenger-safety instruction, and no gps/timeline fact contradicts or confirms the door-opening.

The fare facts returned no records for this dispute type, so I cannot put a computable SGD figure on any refund; the requested outcome is escalate, and weakness lies in the fact that this leaves the $32.86 already charged (fixed fare, no fare facts) with the human reviewer rather than settled here.

claims.assertion: The rider's own message asks to be let out mid-journey (F3, 17:09: "Please stop the car, I want to get out here."), so the dispute is about a mid-ride exit request, not about the fare or the route.

The driver's reply (F4, 17:10: "Sit down or I lock the doors.") is a single instruction given in response to a rider opening a door in motion; the judge must read the words and decide whether they amount to a threat, and there is no policy clause that converts this sentence into an automatic finding against the driver.

A rider attempting to open the door and exit at traffic lights while the trip is in progress is itself a dangerous act on a live carriageway, so the case involves an allegation touching safety of the ride rather than a fare or route overcharge.

Because a threat/intimidation allegation is raised, the correct procedural course is escalation to a human reviewer with a factual summary rather than an automatic ruling, and the driver does not oppose that route.

No money is in dispute: the trip was a fixed-price RydeX fare (complaint: $32.86 quoted up front), the GPS track shows the actual distance 15.4 km against an optimal 15.5 km, i.e. -0.1 km (F1), so no excess distance and no refundable detour mileage exists.

The whole trip was completed and delivered as booked: 15.4 km actual vs 15.5 km optimal (F1) with a duration of 23.7 min against 21.8 min estimated, i.e. +1.9 min (F2), a normal completion with no unexplained stop and no unrecovered deviation.
There is nothing to claw back on the fare side: no off-route segment, no unbilled detour mileage and no traffic-diversion claim arise on this record (F1, F2), so the fare of $32.86 should stand.

The driver has a clean 90-day record — 893 days on the platform, 1038 trips, 0 disputes and 0 upheld (F8) — which is inconsistent with a pattern of intimidating riders and gives no basis for a flag_account action against him.

The rider likewise has no dispute history (F7: 619 days, 0 disputes, 0 upheld), so the conflict is an isolated one-off incident between two otherwise clean accounts, which supports human review over any automated penalty.

weaknesses: The driver's own written words on record are the weakest point of this case: F4 ("Sit down or I lock the doors.") is capable of being read as an intimidation of the rider, and if the judge so reads it under SAFE-1 the case goes to a person regardless of how clean the rest of the record is.

The driver's account of why he spoke (rider tried to open the door at the lights) exists only in his own post-trip statement, F6; the system record contains no door-sensor, in-cabin or camera fact corroborating it, so the 'she opened the door first' justification rests on an uncorroborated statement and may be treated as a claim rather than proof.

F3 shows the rider asked to be let out at 17:09 and the trip nonetheless continued to drop-off at 17:31 (per the trip record), so the other side can argue the driver refused a stop/exit request and effectively held the rider in the car — the +1.9 min duration in F2 gives them a small figure to point at, and RD-3 is the clause they will invoke against the driver's refusal to stop.

Nothing in the driving record helps the driver on the safety point: F1 and F2 show only an ordinary completed trip, so they rebut any fare or route complaint but do not rebut the rider's account of what was said and how she felt.

points.response: I do not contest the characterisation — my client's message at 17:09 asked to be let out (F3) and that is precisely the point: she asked to leave and the recorded reply one minute later was a threat to lock her in (F4), which is a safety matter and not a fare matter; SAFE-1 covers it.

Accepted that the judge reads the words; but the record the judge reads includes the driver's own admission that he refused the exit request and drove on (F6), so the words were backed by the act and by a complete, timestamped chat record (F5) — not a stray sentence.

The door-opening detail appears only in the driver's post-trip statement (F6); no fact in the set corroborates it, and no SAFE-2 fact (collision, injury, dangerous driving) exists, so this cannot be used to convert my client's safety complaint into a finding against her.

Agreed: escalation is the correct course for a threat/intimidation allegation and both sides now ask for it; the human reviewer should get the whole record, including that the rider asked to get out at 17:09 (F3) and the trip ran to 17:31 with a +1.9 min duration (F2).

No refund is sought on this case, so this point is harmless — but the fixed $32.86 fare and the 15.4 vs 15.5 km track (F1) say nothing about what was said in the cabin (F4, F6); the money silence of RD-2/FARE-1 does not answer SAFE-1.

The route was normal, but the trip took 23.7 min against a 21.8 min estimate (F2) while being 0.1 km shorter than optimal (F1), i.e. the clock ran on after my client asked to be let out at 17:09 (F3) — that extra time in a car she asked to leave is the harm she describes, not a route complaint.

Conceded on the fare: no off-route segment or excess mileage exists (F1, F2), so no RD-1/RD-2 refund is asked for; my request is the SAFE-1 escalation only, and I withdraw any suggestion of a fare refund.
Agreed, and I make no flag_account request: the driver's 893-day, 1038-trip, 0-dispute record (F8) means this referral turns on the single recorded exchange (F4), not on a pattern.

Agreed that both accounts are otherwise clean (F7, F8) and human review is right — but a clean history of the driver does not make the words at F4 unrecorded, and the rider's 619-day, 4.8-rating, zero-dispute record (F7) means her account of feeling unsafe is not a pattern-based fabrication.

That the message is a threat is the rider's characterisation, not a recorded fact: F4 is one line spoken after the rider's own request to be let out (F3), and what a sentence means is for the judge to read from the words; the driver asks that it be read against F6, where he says he was answering a rider trying to open a door at the lights. Under SAFE-1 the correct consequence is a screening referral and a factual summary, not an automatic finding against the driver, and the driver does not resist that referral.

C2 is not contested as far as it goes: the chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F5) and F4 stands on the record — but a complete, timestamped record proves only what was written, not that the words amounted to intimidation, since F6 shows the driver's stated reason (rider opening the door in motion) and no system fact — no gps, timeline or door-sensor fact — contradicts or confirms either reading.

The driver agrees with the rider on the remedy: this is an escalate case, so the words in F4 go to a human reviewer with the fact summary and no automatic penalty is imposed; the driver asks only that the summary be neutral, recording that F4 followed the rider's request in F3 and that F6 gives the driver's reason, without the rider's 'coercion of a passenger in a moving vehicle' label being adopted as a finding.

C4 reverses the arithmetic: the 23.7 min duration against a 21.8 min estimate (F2) occurred on a route that was 0.1 km SHORTER than optimal (F1), i.e. -0.1 km / -0%, so there is no off-route segment, no unexplained diversion and no detour mileage to explain; a 1.9-minute longer run over an unchanged corridor is ordinary traffic behaviour on a fixed-price fare (F1, F2) and cannot be converted into a finding of unsafe confinement under SAFE-1.

The rider's clean profile (F7: 619 days, rating 4.8, 0 disputes in 90 days) is accepted and is not needed against her, but a clean account is not corroboration of the incident — profile facts can never decide a case, and the only incident-related record remains the single chat line F4 read together with the driver's explanation F6.

The rider's concession on the driver's clean record is noted and the driver relies on it: 893 days, 1038 trips, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days (F8) is inconsistent with a pattern of intimidating passengers and gives no basis for any flag_account action; the driver's own position is equally that this cabin incident goes to a human under SAFE-1 and nothing else.
